case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.limits: The Court addressed one licensing use of one image and expressly did not decide the status of the original Warhol series, so its reach beyond commercial licensing disputes is still being worked out.
case.holding: The first fair use factor asks whether the challenged use shares the same purpose as the original, especially where both are licensed into the same market. Adding new meaning or message is not by itself enough.

case.why_ai_cites_it: The most important recent decision cutting against AI defendants, and the reason a training defense cannot rest on the word transformative alone. Plaintiffs cite it for the proposition that a system competing in the market the original was licensed into looks like substitution rather than transformation.

reading.body:
Warhol v. Goldsmith, a 2023 Supreme Court decision, is the most important recent precedent working against AI defendants specifically, cited by plaintiffs in the litigation record here rather than by the companies being sued.

Where most of this collection's precedents are cited by defense to argue that AI training is transformative, this one is cited by plaintiffs for nearly the opposite proposition, that a system competing in the same market the original was licensed into looks like substitution rather than transformation. That the two most commonly cited fair-use precedents in this entire set, this one and Campbell v. Acuff-Rose, point in opposite directions is itself the clearest evidence that the transformative-use question in AI training litigation remains genuinely unsettled rather than leaning one way.

The case explicitly did not decide the status of the original Warhol series itself, so its reach beyond commercial licensing disputes specifically is, by the Court's own statement, still being worked out.
